new_statements.rule_in_words: For Sea Dayak (Iban) of the Batang Lupar tribes, Balau explicitly included: most words are disyllabic and the accent generally falls on the first (= penultimate) syllable; nothing is said about longer words. The fuller modern Iban statements conflict: Richards 1981 (pp. xiv-xv) gives penultimate stress unless the penult vowel is e/schwa (then final), unaffected by affixation; Asmah Haji Omar 1969/1981 (section 2.6, the catalog's iban1264 source) gives final stress, non-phonemic, as an intonation element; Scott 1957 (Second Division speakers) reports slightly increased stress on the final syllable in isolation forms. No source describes Balau speech separately.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Howell & Bailey; Richards 1981 mentions only 'even' stress on penult and final in closed-final words with a penultimate e; StressTyp2 (from Asmah 1981) records no secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Howell & Bailey: only the hedge 'generally'. Richards 1981: penultimate e (schwa) shifts stress to the final; written-but-unpronounced e after r (ter-e-bai = TER-bai); eN+C penults keep stress (EM-pa', REN-tap); pengap invocation recital has 'greatly varied' stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Howell & Bailey speak of the word ('Dyak words.. the accented syllable'); Scott 1957 explicitly describes citation forms in isolation (slight final prominence); Asmah 1969 treats stress as a non-phonemic intonation element assigned to emphasised words (the catalog classes iban1264 as word and phrase together word/phrase). The statement applies to Iban as a whole; Balau is covered only as one of the tribes within the dictionary's stated scope.
new_statements.identity_note: bala1306 'Balau' is a Glottolog Bookkeeping entry: ISO 639-3 [blg] was retired by Change Request 2020-042 (Anderbeck & Anonby) and merged into Iban [iba] (iban1264): "Balau seemingly was never a distinct language, but rather a somewhat-central Sarawak Iban dialect.. Lexical and phonological tests place it within the Iban mainstream." Balau = the Iban of the lower Batang Lupar / Lingga (Banting) area, Second (Sri Aman) Division, Sarawak. No description of Balau speech as such exists; every stress statement found is for Sea Dayak / Iban as a whole (iban1264), whose Second-Division base includes the Balau area. Iban is already in the catalog (catalog record, the deciding source Asmah Haji Omar 1969 section 2.6 pp. 69-70, final stress, non-phonemic). Cataloguing bala1306 separately would double-count Iban under a retired code, hence not proposed for the catalog even though a first-hand statement covering Balau was quoted from a saved file.

new_statements.quote: For the purpose of this thesis, intonation is regarded as comprising stress, pitch and vowel quantity. These three elements are not phonemic. The stress is considered as the primary intonation element, as a heavy stress is usually accompanied by a high pitch and a longer duration of the vowel which forms the nucleus of the stressed syllable. [p. 70:] Stress in Iban always falls on the final syllable of a word. Any word receiving emphasis, with or without an emphasizing word (cf. 4.37), is stressed. At the end of a sentence, the intonation forms a contour which is either falling or rising.

[viii]: most words disyllabic, 'the accented syllable is generally the first' = initial/penult). new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the final syllable of every word; stress, pitch and length are treated as non-phonemic intonation elements, with the stressed syllable also carrying high pitch and a longer vowel. Emphasis (with or without an emphasizing word) puts a heavy stress on the whole word; imperative intonation puts a heavy stress on the verb and exclamative intonation on the exclaimed word.
new_statements.exceptions: None for word stress ('always'). Sentence-level heavy stress for emphasis, imperatives and exclamations is described as an intonation phenomenon (section 2.6, p. 70), not as a lexical exception.
new_statements.identity_note: Balau is a Sea Dayak (Iban) dialect of the Batang Lupar and Lingga rivers (Banting area), Second Division, Sarawak; ISO 639-3 change request 2020-042 merged [blg] into Iban [iba] on the ground that Balau 'was never a distinct language, but rather a somewhat-central Sarawak Iban dialect'. Neither work opened describes Balau separately: Asmah 1969/1981 describes Iban as a whole from Third Division (Sibu, Kanowit, Kapit) and First/Second Division (Kuching, Betong) recordings and treats the dialects as homogeneous, mentioning Balau only as the self-designation /kami balaw/; Scott 1957 describes the pronunciation of Second Division speakers generally.

new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the existing Howell & Bailey 1900 statement (first syllable of disyllables) and Richards 1981 (penult unless e); agrees with Asmah 1969/1981 (final) and with the Iban (iban1264) catalog record. Scott's speakers are from the Second Division, the administrative division that contains the Balau area (Batang Lupar/Lingga), but he describes Sea Dayak generally, not the Balau dialect specifically. The listed open_url (WALS refdb record) is only a bibliographic record; the DOI resolves to a Cambridge Core abstract page with 'Access options', and the PDF link redirects to that same page, so the full text is not open.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words spoken in isolation carry slightly increased stress on the final syllable (Second Division Sea Dayak speakers). Whether the body of the article qualifies this (e.g. for words with a penultimate schwa) could not be checked: only the abstract was accessible.

new_statements.quote: [p. 509] The following notes on the phonetic interpretation of this spelling are based on the pronunciation of speakers from the Second Division of Sarawak. The descriptions refer to words spoken in isolation, which have slightly increased stress on the final syllable. [p. 510, sec. 1] In words written with e in the penultimate syllable, the pronunciation has either a weak central vowel or (most commonly when a liquid follows) no vowel-sound in that syllable [...] [p. 512, sec. 9] In the pronunciation of words of more than two syllables, the syllables preceding the penult have either a weak central vowel or no vowel-sound, thus pematang, pəmataŋ, ‘an embankment’
new_statements.citation: Scott, N. C. 1957. Notes on the pronunciation of Sea Dayak. Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 20(1): 509-512.

new_statements.relation_note: No catalog record for bala1306. The full text confirms, verbatim on p. 509, the Scott 1957 statement already held by the project (fixed final, words in isolation) and adds no further stress rule; consistent with Asmah 1969/1981 ('Stress in Iban always falls on the final syllable of a word'); stands against Richards 1981 (penult unless e) and the unclear Howell & Bailey 1900 'Accent' note, as already recorded. New compatible detail only: schwa/zero in the penult written e and in all pre-penultimate syllables (secs. 1, 9). Language-level Sea Dayak/Iban description (Second Division speakers), not Balau-specific.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Sea Dayak (Iban) words spoken in isolation, as pronounced by Second Division speakers, carry slightly increased stress on the final syllable. The article is otherwise a segment-by-segment key to Scott's systematic spelling; its only other prosodically relevant remarks are that orthographic e in the penult is a weak central vowel or is dropped (esp. before a liquid: beras = bəras or bras), that all syllables before the penult have a weak central vowel or no vowel at all (with long initial consonants as an alternative: gegudi = gəgode or g:ode), and that final open vowels are relatively long. No other statement on stress placement, and none restricting the final-stress remark to particular word types.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned anywhere in the article (pp. 509-512 read in full)
new_statements.exceptions: none; the final-stress remark is qualified only by its domain ('words spoken in isolation', 'slightly increased'). Sec. 4 notes that in kain the close vowel has 'relatively low prominence' (käin heard as kajen), a vowel-sequence remark, not a stress exception.
new_statements.identity_note: Scott describes Sea Dayak (Iban) as pronounced by speakers from the Second Division of Sarawak, the division containing the Balau (Batang Lupar/Lingga) area, not the Balau dialect specifically; Balau was merged into Iban by ISO 639-3 CR 2020-042.

readall_conflicts: The sources for Sea Dayak/Iban (of which Balau is a dialect) disagree on placement. Howell & Bailey 1900 (the existing statement for this key, Grammatical Synopsis p. [viii]) say 'the accented syllable is generally the first' of the typical disyllable, and Richards 1981 (An Iban-English Dictionary pp. xiv-xv, held) gives a detailed penultimate rule 'unless the vowel is e', with listed exceptions; Adelaar 1992 (Proto-Malayic 2.5.1) follows Richards. 70) and Scott 1957 (abstract: words in isolation 'have slightly increased stress on the final syllable', Second Division speakers). Asmah also states that stress, pitch and quantity 'are not phonemic', and Scott calls the final prominence 'slightly increased', so the final-stress claims are weak, isolation-form observations that may reflect phrase-final lengthening rather than lexical stress; the penult-vs-final disagreement is unresolved by anything read here. None of the sources describes the Balau dialect specifically. No catalog record exists for bala1306. Nothing new was read: the only accessible text of Scott 1957 remains its opening paragraph (words in isolation have slightly increased stress on the final syllable), which agrees with Asmah 1969/1981 (stress always on the final syllable) and with the Scott 1957 statement already held by the project, and stands against the Howell & Bailey 1900 'Accent' note (filed as unclear) and Richards 1981 (penult unless e, per the iban1264 holdings).
